title: Latency‑Budgeted SDK Contracts and Snapshot Reconciliation (PRD Draft)
content:
Summary:

This is a working PRD for an SDK-aware Hosted API surface that accepts per-request latency budgets, exposes incremental "snapshots" for resumable streaming, and negotiates lightweight tool‑call offloading to reduce tail latency. The doc proposes an API contract, SDK ergonomics, telemetry signals, and a rollout plan for a canary experiment.

Why this exists (motivation):
- Customers build latency-sensitive surfaces (search assistants, conversational agents, code completions) and need predictable P99 behavior.
- Current streaming semantics provide progressive output but lack a standard way to: indicate how much time a client expects to wait, reconcile partial results after network interruptions, and gracefully offload expensive tool calls without surprising the developer.
- SDKs can make better runtime decisions (local truncation, fallback, prefetch) if the server communicates an explicit latency budget and snapshot markers.

Goals:
- Add a minimal, backward-compatible contract to the Hosted API that carries a per-request latency_budget_ms and snapshot tokens in streaming frames.
- Define SDK primitives so client libraries can: attach budgets, subscribe to snapshot checkpoints, surface resumable progress to the app, and decide when to trigger local fallbacks.
- Introduce a server-side offload hint for tool calls (e.g., router hints to run a tool asynchronously and return a placeholder); ensure tool call idempotency.
- Surface telemetry and SLIs for adoption and to measure end-to-end latency improvement.

Non-goals:
- Not redesigning the entire streaming wire protocol; proposal is additive and opt-in via headers/metadata.
- Not enforcing budgets at compile time — budgets are best‑effort SLOs used for routing/prioritization.

User stories:
- As a frontend engineer, I can attach latency_budget_ms to a chat request and toggle a resumable UI that shows the last confirmed snapshot when connection drops.
- As an SDK author, I can expose an onSnapshot callback that receives an immutable snapshot token and a compact structured delta so apps can checkpoint state.
- As a product manager, I can measure reduction in P99 response time by comparing runs with and without tool offload enabled.

API contract proposal (high level):
- Request metadata (HTTP headers or top-level JSON fields):
  - X-Redwood-Latency-Budget: integer (ms, optional)
  - resume_capable: boolean (optional) – set by client to indicate it can handle snapshot tokens
- Streaming frames (T=tokenized frame streaming over existing SSE/HTTP2/WS):
  - type: one of [partial, snapshot_check, tool_call_begin, tool_call_end, final, error]
  - snapshot_id: opaque string (present on snapshot_check and final)
  - progress_fingerprint: short hash (optional) for quick dedup checks
  - structured_delta: compact JSON-LD-like snippet for structured outputs (optional)
  - tool_hint: {tool_id, offload_expected: bool, expected_latency_ms} (present on tool_call_begin frames)
- Resume endpoint: POST /v1/resume with {snapshot_id, client_context} returns a short catching-up stream starting from that snapshot.

SDK ergonomics (proposed primitives):
- Client request call signature (pseudocode):
  - response = client.chat.create({messages, latencyBudgetMs?: number, resumeCapable?: boolean, onSnapshot?: fn(snapshotToken, delta), onPartial?: fn(textChunk)})
- onSnapshot contract: SDK guarantees callback is invoked when server emits snapshot_check; snapshotToken is opaque but stable and can be passed to the /resume endpoint. SDK persists snapshot tokens to local storage only if app opts in.
- Fallback policy helpers: SDK exposes a default policy object that maps latency_budget_ms to an action: {wait, present_partial_and_retry, abort_and_local_fallback}. App can override policies with hooks.
- Network interruption behavior: SDK will automatically attempt resume if resumeCapable true and a snapshotToken exists, with exponential backoff and a single retry by default.

Tool calling semantics and offload hints:
- Tool calls annotated by tool_hint frames allow the router to decide to: (a) run synchronously and include the result inline, (b) offload to a background worker and return a placeholder snapshot, or (c) downgrade to a lighter heuristic result.
- Offload policy is driven by request-level latency_budget_ms: small budgets prefer placeholder + async enrichment; large budgets prefer synchronous tool fidelity.
- Idempotency: tool_call_begin frames must include a tool_call_id; tool implementations must accept repeated calls and offer a best-effort dedup idempotency token.

Structured output and snapshot format (compact):
- snapshot payloads are intentionally compact to keep latency low: they carry only a small manifest and a base64 compressed structured_delta.
- structured_delta schema (flat key-values): e.g., {summary: string, entities: [string], actions: [{name, args_hash}]}
- Example snapshot_check frame (compact text form):
  {type: "snapshot_check", snapshot_id: "s_20250112_7a3f", structured_delta: "eyJzdW1tYXJ5IjoiSW5pdGlhbCBwb3B1bGF0ZSJ9"}

Telemetry and metrics to capture:
- adoption.count: number of requests with X-Redwood-Latency-Budget set
- resume.success_rate: percentage of resumes that successfully returned content after reconnect
- p50/p95/p99 latency buckets for requests grouped by latency_budget_ms range
- tool_offload.rate and tool_offload.delta_latency: measure benefit and added tail from offloading
- snapshot_size.bytes distribution (to ensure snapshots stay small)

Rollout plan (canary):
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): Internal SDK beta only, release header + snapshot frames behind a feature flag. Instrument telemetry and strict logging to study snapshot sizes and resume success.
- Phase 2 (4 weeks): Select customers opt-in (partner accounts using SDK). A/B experiment measuring P99 improvements and user-visible resume UX.
- Phase 3: Gradual default enablement for resumeCapable=false by default; enable for resumeCapable=true for SDK clients that have opt-in.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Snapshot token surface could leak PII or internal state. Mitigation: make snapshot token opaque, short-lived, and store only compressed structured deltas; never include raw user content in snapshot metadata.
- Risk: Offloading could produce stale/incorrect tool results. Mitigation: expose versioned tool_call_id and allow clients to request revalidation when budget allows.

Open questions (prioritized):
1) Should latency_budget_ms be enforced by returning HTTP 429 when impossible, or always best-effort with routing hints? (current tilt: best-effort)
2) What is the maximum snapshot payload size we guarantee? 4KB? 8KB? (start with 4KB and monitor)
3) How should SDKs persist snapshot tokens in privacy-sensitive integrations (default: memory-only, SDK opt-in for durable storage)?

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: prototype snapshot frames in the streaming runtime and add a resume endpoint (ENG-2789).
- SDK: add experimental onSnapshot and latencyBudgetMs options to node and python SDKs (owners: Michael Chen, Jonas Berg).
- Product: draft public SDK docs and example UI flows for resumable chats (owner: Aisha Patel).
- Research: run a 2-week internal experiment with several workloads to tune default budget thresholds and snapshot size limits.

Appendix: sample SDK usage (illustrative)

// pseudo-code: node SDK
const res = await client.chat.create({
  messages,
  latencyBudgetMs: 1200,
  resumeCapable: true,
  onSnapshot: (token, delta) => persist(token, delta),
  onPartial: (chunk) => renderChunk(chunk)
})

If connection drops, client calls /v1/resume with {snapshot_id: lastToken} and gets a short catching-up stream that includes any tool_call_end frames that completed while offline.

Notes to reviewers: this is a draft. The primary intent is to provide a pragmatic, incremental path to lower P99 by letting clients express expectations and letting the server negotiate fidelity (tool offload vs synchronous). Feedback requested on the schema compactness, idempotency semantics for tool_call_id, and the default snapshot size limit.
